questions.hook: He fainted on the stairs. That single detail decides the question.
questions.key_finding: Carotid upstroke: delayed and low amplitude
questions.short_vignette: A 74-year-old man collapses while climbing the stairs and recovers within a minute. He has a harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids, and a delayed, low-amplitude carotid upstroke.
questions.vignette: A 74-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a 6-month history of shortness of breath with exertion. Last week he lost consciousness while climbing the stairs to his apartment and recovered within a minute. He has no chest pain. Blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, pulse 72/min. Cardiac examination shows a harsh, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur loudest at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotid arteries. The second heart sound is soft. The carotid upstroke is delayed and low in amplitude. The lungs are clear and there is no peripheral edema.
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's loss of consciousness?

options.text: Fixed stroke volume limiting the rise in cardiac output during exertion
options.why: A stenotic valve cannot open wider when demand rises. At rest the stiff ventricle still generates adequate output; on exertion stroke volume is capped, cardiac output fails to rise, and cerebral perfusion falls.
options.would_make_right: Nothing - this is the correct mechanism for exertional syncope with a fixed outflow obstruction.

options.why: Calcific aortic stenosis can extend into the conduction system, but a block is not load-dependent and does not wait for the stairs.
options.would_make_right: Syncope occurring at rest, or an ECG showing wide-complex bradycardia with absent P waves.

options.text: Ventricular arrhythmia arising from myocardial scar
options.why: Arrhythmic syncope classically has no warning and no reproducible exertional trigger. This patient's syncope is exertion-linked, which points to a haemodynamic cause.
options.would_make_right: Syncope without prodrome, family history of sudden cardiac death, scar on echocardiography, or a prolonged QT interval.

options.text: Vasovagal reflex triggered by increased intrathoracic pressure
options.why: Vasovagal syncope has a prodrome of warmth, nausea and tunnel vision, is provoked by heat, pain or prolonged standing, and does not produce a fixed low-amplitude carotid upstroke.
options.would_make_right: A clear prodrome, syncope while standing, rapid full recovery, and a normal cardiac examination.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension from reduced intravascular volume
options.why: There is no volume loss, no diuretic use, and no positional trigger. Orthostatic syncope occurs within seconds of standing, not after climbing stairs.
options.would_make_right: A documented postural blood pressure drop, diuretic use or dehydration, and syncope on standing.

questions.rule: Exertional syncope is a haemodynamic problem until proven otherwise: the heart cannot meet demand. Aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension are the three causes.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1, Cardiology - Valvular disease
2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease

questions.hook: A 95% sensitive test. An 8.8% chance you actually have the disease.
questions.short_vignette: A screening test has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. The disease affects 1% of the population. A patient tests positive.
questions.vignette: A new screening test for a disease has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 90%. The disease has a prevalence of 1% in the population being screened.
questions.stem: If a person from this population tests positive, what is the probability that they actually have the disease?

options.why: In 10,000 people, 100 have the disease and 95 of those test positive; of the 9,900 without disease, 990 test positive falsely. Of 1,085 positives only 95 are true, giving 95/1,085 = 8.8%.
options.would_make_right: Nothing - this is the correct predictive value at 1% prevalence.

options.why: This is the sensitivity, which answers the opposite question: among people who have the disease, what fraction test positive.
options.would_make_right: A question asking for the proportion of diseased patients who test positive, not the proportion of positives who are diseased.

options.why: This is the specificity: among people who are well, what fraction test negative. It ignores prevalence and runs in the wrong direction.
options.would_make_right: A question asking what fraction of healthy people test negative.

options.why: A 50% positive predictive value would require prevalence high enough to balance the false positive rate. At 1% prevalence the false positives swamp the true positives.
options.would_make_right: A prevalence roughly equal to the false positive rate, which at these test characteristics is about 10%.

options.why: This is the false positive rate applied to the whole population, not a predictive value. It answers no question that was asked.
options.would_make_right: A question asking for the probability that a healthy person tests positive, which is 10% here, not 0.9%.

questions.rule: Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test. Predictive values belong to the patient in front of you, and they move with prevalence. Never answer a predictive-value question before writing down the prevalence.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1, Biostatistics - Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values

questions.hook: Platelets 18,000. Every instinct says transfuse. That instinct is wrong.
questions.short_vignette: A 29-year-old woman has five days of bruising and confusion. Platelets 18,000, haemoglobin 7.4, schistocytes on the smear, PT and aPTT both normal, creatinine 1.1.
questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes in with five days of fatigue and easy bruising, and her husband says she has been confused since this morning. Temperature 37.8 C. There are petechiae over both shins. She is not pregnant and takes no medications. Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, platelets 18,000/uL, reticulocytes 9%, lactate dehydrogenase 900 U/L, indirect bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. PT/INR and aPTT are both normal. Peripheral smear shows schistocytes. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein and no red cells.
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.why: Plasma exchange removes the autoantibody against ADAMTS13 and replaces the enzyme at the same time. Untreated TTP carries high mortality and the response window is measured in hours.
options.would_make_right: Nothing - plasma exchange is first-line for suspected TTP with neurologic involvement.

options.why: Every transfused platelet is fuel for further microthrombi. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP unless there is life-threatening bleeding or imminent surgery.
options.would_make_right: Active life-threatening haemorrhage, intracranial bleeding, or a patient going to the operating room immediately.

options.why: Eculizumab blocks complement C5 and treats atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, which is renal-predominant with a rising creatinine and normal ADAMTS13 activity. This patient's creatinine is 1.1.
options.would_make_right: Renal-predominant disease with rapidly rising creatinine, dialysis requirement, and normal ADAMTS13 activity.

options.why: Vitamin K treats coagulopathy, which prolongs the PT. This patient's PT and aPTT are both normal, so there is no coagulation factor deficiency to correct.
options.would_make_right: A prolonged PT or INR, as in warfarin use, liver disease or fat malabsorption.

options.why: TTP is a medical emergency. Observation without plasma exchange was associated with mortality above 90% historically and remains unacceptable today.
options.would_make_right: A stable patient with no red cell destruction, which is not this picture.

questions.rule: Microangiopathic haemolysis plus thrombocytopenia plus normal coagulation studies equals a thrombotic microangiopathy. Platelets are contraindicated and plasma exchange is the treatment: today, not tomorrow.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1, Hematology - Thrombotic microangiopathies
ISTH Guidelines for the Management of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura

questions.hook: It says to wait for antibiotics—so you order cultures after starting them, right?
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with a history of aortic valve replacement presents with 2 days of fever and chills. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. Vitals: T 39.6°C, HR 118/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 22/min. Labs: WBC 15,200/mm3. Two sets of blood cultures are drawn. He receives empiric IV antibiotics immediately afterward. Cultures later grow gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which next action best improves diagnostic yield while also addressing sepsis?
questions.short_vignette: Man with suspected endocarditis: after drawing cultures and starting antibiotics, what improves diagnostic yield?
questions.stem: To maximize the likelihood of identifying the causative organism in suspected infective endocarditis, what should be done regarding blood cultures and antibiotics?

options.text: Obtain multiple blood cultures before giving any antibiotics
options.why: Culturing before antimicrobial therapy maximizes the chance that organisms will grow. In suspected infective endocarditis with sepsis, draw cultures urgently and then start empiric antibiotics without delay.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette so antibiotics are started before blood cultures are drawn; then correct it by specifying cultures are obtained immediately before antibiotics.

options.text: Start antibiotics immediately and delay blood cultures until vitals stabilize
options.why: Antibiotics rapidly reduce culture positivity. Delaying cultures lowers diagnostic yield and risks missing the opportunity to isolate the pathogen, which is crucial in endocarditis.
options.would_make_right: Alter the vignette so blood cultures were drawn only after several hours of antibiotics and then choose the corrected approach of drawing cultures before antibiotics.

options.text: Order only a single blood culture set because endocarditis is persistent
options.why: Bacteremia can be intermittent; multiple sets from different venipuncture sites increase the probability of capturing organisms. A single set risks false-negative results.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to include only one blood culture set; then make the correct option correct by revising it to multiple sets drawn before antibiotics.

options.text: Use transthoracic echocardiography first and skip blood cultures since echo detects infection
options.why: Echocardiography supports diagnosis but does not identify the organism. Blood cultures are essential to guide targeted therapy and determine the causative pathogen.
options.would_make_right: Revise the vignette to state that blood cultures are not obtained; then the correct action becomes obtaining blood cultures promptly before antibiotics.

options.text: Discontinue antibiotics after cultures are drawn because the organism will regrow
options.why: Stopping antibiotics after cultures does not reliably allow regrowth and is dangerous in septic patients. Ongoing therapy is required while culture results and susceptibilities are pending.
options.would_make_right: Modify the vignette to say antibiotics are stopped after cultures; then the corrected diagnostic-yield strategy would still require starting only after cultures are drawn and continuing empiric therapy.

questions.rule: In suspected infective endocarditis, draw multiple blood cultures urgently before starting antibiotics to preserve culture yield while treating sepsis immediately afterward.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Infectious Disease/Endocarditis
IDSA Infective Endocarditis guideline (blood culture timing)

questions.hook: He says, 'My son’s bruises started after a dental procedure—so he must have von Willebrand disease,' right?
questions.key_finding: Prolonged isolated aPTT with normal platelets
questions.vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought for frequent bruising and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts. His mother reports that after dental work 2 weeks ago, he had persistent gum bleeding for 2 days. He has no epistaxis or petechiae. Vitals are normal. Exam shows large ecchymoses on the legs. CBC shows platelets 240,000/mm3. PT is 11.2 seconds (normal). aPTT is 68 seconds (markedly prolonged). Mixing study fails to correct. No joint deformities are noted yet. The child is otherwise healthy.
questions.short_vignette: 6-year-old boy with large bruises and prolonged post-dental bleeding; platelets normal; PT normal; isolated prolonged aPTT not corrected by mixing.
questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the coagulation abnormality?

options.text: Hemophilia A due to factor VIII deficiency
options.why: Hemophilia A causes impaired intrinsic pathway clotting, leading to an isolated prolonged aPTT with normal platelet count and PT. Failure of a mixing study to correct suggests a true factor deficiency pattern consistent with hemophilia rather than factor inhibitor presence.
options.would_make_right: Add a history of similar bleeding in maternal relatives and specify that aPTT does not correct with mixing due to factor VIII deficiency (not an inhibitor).

options.why: von Willebrand disease typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia) and often shows prolonged bleeding time with variable aPTT prolongation. It would not classically produce a markedly prolonged isolated aPTT with normal PT and normal platelets as the primary abnormality.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignettes bleeding pattern to include recurrent epistaxis and note decreased von Willebrand factor activity with reduced factor VIII secondary effects.

options.why: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a platelet function disorder with normal PT and typically normal or mildly affected aPTT, not a markedly prolonged isolated aPTT. It causes mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet counts but impaired aggregation.
options.would_make_right: Keep PT and aPTT normal but add painless mucosal bleeding with normal platelet count and abnormal platelet aggregation testing.

options.text: Acquired hemophilia due to factor VIII inhibitor
options.why: Acquired hemophilia usually occurs in older adults or postpartum and causes severe bleeding with a prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing due to an inhibitor. The patient is a young boy with no trigger described, making inherited hemophilia more likely.
options.would_make_right: Change the patient to a 70-year-old (or postpartum patient) and add a new, sudden onset of bleeding with no family history, consistent with an acquired inhibitor.

options.why: DIC typically causes thrombocytopenia and both PT and aPTT prolongation due to consumption of multiple clotting factors. This patient has normal platelets and a normal PT, arguing strongly against DIC.
options.would_make_right: Lower platelets to ~30,000/mm3 and prolong PT as well (eg, both PT and aPTT markedly increased) with clinical sepsis or trauma.

questions.rule: Isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT and normal platelets points to intrinsic factor problems (eg hemophilia) rather than platelet disorders or vitamin K deficiency.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Coagulation Disorders
UpToDate review of hemophilia and mixing studies

questions.hook: Proteinuria alone is not enough—spot the missing criterion for preeclampsia.
questions.vignette: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks’ gestation presents with headache and mild swelling of her face. Blood pressure is 162/104 mmHg on two measurements 4 hours apart. Urinalysis shows protein 1+ with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.3. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Platelets are 240,000/µL. AST is 22 U/L and ALT is 24 U/L. She has no right upper quadrant pain and no visual changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.short_vignette: At 28 weeks, BP 162/104 mmHg with urine protein/Cr 0.3 and normal platelets/AST/ALT/creatinine.
questions.stem: At 28 weeks’ gestation, she has new-onset hypertension but no evidence of end-organ dysfunction; what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.why: Preeclampsia requires hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria meeting threshold or end-organ dysfunction (eg, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, or persistent neurologic symptoms). Her protein-to-creatinine ratio is below the diagnostic cutoff and labs are normal.
options.would_make_right: Increase urine protein-to-creatinine ratio to ≥0.3 with a clearly measured quantitative protein level, or add end-organ findings such as platelets 90,000/µL or creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.

options.why: Gestational hypertension is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria meeting criteria and without end-organ dysfunction. Her protein/Cr ratio is 0.3 and she has normal platelets, creatinine, and transaminases.
options.would_make_right: Change the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio to 0.1 (or remove proteinuria findings) while keeping BP and end-organ labs the same.

options.why: Chronic hypertension is present before 20 weeks or before pregnancy is known to have started, or persists beyond 12 weeks postpartum. This case begins at 28 weeks.
options.would_make_right: Specify that her blood pressure was ≥140/90 mmHg before 20 weeks’ gestation or earlier in the current pregnancy.

options.why: HELLP requires hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. She has normal platelets and normal transaminases, with no evidence of hemolysis.
options.would_make_right: Lower platelets to <100,000/µL and elevate AST/ALT to >2× the upper limit, adding hemolysis markers (eg, elevated LDH and schistocytes).

options.why: This condition typically presents in the third trimester with hepatic dysfunction (markedly elevated transaminases), coagulopathy, and sometimes hypoglycemia. Her AST/ALT are normal and no coagulopathy is provided.
options.would_make_right: Add hepatic failure clues such as AST/ALT significantly elevated with an INR elevation (or hypoglycemia) while keeping hypertension present.

questions.rule: In pregnancy, diagnose preeclampsia only when hypertension after 20 weeks is accompanied by significant proteinuria and/or end-organ dysfunction.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Obstetrics: Preeclampsia and Gestational Hypertension
ACOG Practice Bulletin (Preeclampsia and Related Disorders)

questions.hook: He says, “My kidneys will be fine again once I stop the medication,” but what do labs show?
questions.key_finding: Low FENa with high urine osmolality
questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with chronic heart failure presents with 2 days of poor oral intake and dizziness after starting a new diuretic. He has dry mucous membranes. Vitals: BP 88/54 mmHg, HR 102/min, RR 18/min, T 36.8°C. Labs show creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0) and BUN 42 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no casts. Urine studies: urine sodium 18 mEq/L, urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg. After IV fluids, his urine output improves over several hours.
questions.short_vignette: Elderly on diuretics with dehydration: creatinine up, no casts. Urine Na low (18), urine osm high (620) after fluids improve output.
questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains his acute kidney injury?

options.text: Prerenal azotemia from decreased renal perfusion
options.why: Prerenal AKI is characterized by intact tubular function, leading to avid sodium and water reabsorption. Low urine sodium and high urine osmolality support this.
options.would_make_right: Change urine sodium to 18 mEq/L (already low) and add “no granular casts” to the urinalysis; keep dehydration and hypotension unchanged.

options.text: Acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxin injury
options.why: ATN typically causes impaired tubular sodium reabsorption, yielding higher urine sodium and often granular casts. This patient’s urine sodium is low and urinalysis shows no casts.
options.would_make_right: Replace urine sodium 18 mEq/L with 60 mEq/L and add “muddy brown granular casts” to urinalysis; keep hypotension history but remove dehydration as the dominant finding.

options.why: Postrenal AKI often presents with urinary retention symptoms or flank pain and can show hydronephrosis. The vignette emphasizes dehydration/hypotension and shows rapid improvement with fluids.
options.would_make_right: Add decreased urine output with suprapubic fullness and flank pain; include renal ultrasound showing bilateral hydronephrosis.

options.why: Intrinsic glomerular disease would more likely produce hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts and proteinuria. Urinalysis here shows no casts and no hematuria is described.
options.would_make_right: Add urinalysis with “RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs” plus proteinuria; do not include the dehydration/hypotension response to fluids.

options.text: Renal artery stenosis causing ischemic nephropathy
options.why: Renal artery stenosis often presents with refractory hypertension and can show asymmetric kidney size or elevated renovascular indices. This patient is hypotensive with dehydration and improves with volume repletion.
options.would_make_right: Change BP to 170/96 mmHg and add “abdominal bruit” with ultrasound showing small, atrophic kidney; remove the poor oral intake/dehydration narrative.

questions.rule: Low urine sodium with concentrated urine suggests prerenal azotemia; ATN shows higher urine sodium and casts.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Renal Physiology
FENa interpretation (prerenal vs ATN) and urine concentration/casts

questions.hook: She has hyperkalemia and low sodium—don't confuse Addison disease with adrenal crisis from secondary causes.
questions.vignette: A 42-year-old woman with progressive fatigue and weight loss reports dizziness when standing. She also has nausea and craving salt. Exam shows mild hyperpigmentation of the knuckles. Vitals: BP 86/54 mmHg, HR 102/min. Labs: Na 128 mEq/L, K 6.1 mEq/L, glucose 68 mg/dL. Morning serum cortisol is 4.2 µg/dL. Plasma ACTH is 860 pg/mL.
questions.short_vignette: Hypotension, hyperpigmentation, Na 128, K 6.1, cortisol 4.2; ACTH 860.
questions.stem: Which endocrine diagnosis best explains her laboratory pattern?

options.why: Primary adrenal failure lowers cortisol, removing negative feedback and causing markedly elevated ACTH. High ACTH also drives increased melanocyte stimulation, explaining hyperpigmentation.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to describe chronic adrenal destruction and keep ACTH markedly elevated with low cortisol.

options.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency due to pituitary failure
options.why: Secondary causes reduce cortisol but do not significantly increase ACTH, so hyperpigmentation would be absent and hyperkalemia would be less prominent.
options.would_make_right: Replace the ACTH result with low or normal ACTH (e.g., ACTH 10 pg/mL) while keeping low cortisol.

options.why: Thyroid storm causes hyperthermia, tachycardia, and agitation; it does not cause the specific cortisol–ACTH pattern or hyperkalemia from aldosterone deficiency.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to include fever and severe tachyarrhythmia with normal electrolytes and a normal cortisol/ACTH pattern.

options.why: Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic hypertension, palpitations, and diaphoresis; it does not produce low cortisol with elevated ACTH or hyperpigmentation.
options.would_make_right: Add paroxysmal headaches and sustained hypertension with normal sodium and potassium and remove cortisol/ACTH abnormalities.

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency
options.why: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency often causes androgen excess and typically presents earlier in life; the vignette describes adult-onset symptoms without virilization or androgen-related findings.
options.would_make_right: Add a history of childhood onset with signs of androgen excess (eg, early pubarche/virilization) while keeping cortisol low and ACTH high.

questions.rule: Low cortisol with high ACTH and hyperpigmentation indicates primary adrenal insufficiency.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine (Adrenal Cortex Disorders)
Guideline: Endocrine Society clinical guidance on adrenal insufficiency diagnosis (ACTH/cortisol interpretation)

questions.hook: He says his new thirst proves type 2 diabetes, but consider ketones instead?
questions.vignette: A 19-year-old man presents with 1 week of increasing thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss. He has nausea and abdominal discomfort. Vitals show BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 112/min, RR 24/min, and T 37.0°C. Labs: glucose 465 mg/dL, serum bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, anion gap 22 mEq/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated. Serum potassium is 5.1 mEq/L. Urinalysis shows glucose and ketones. What is the most likely pathophysiologic defect driving his condition?
questions.short_vignette: 19-year-old with glucose 465, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate.
questions.stem: Which defect best explains his current presentation?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.why: Type 1 diabetes causes insulin deficiency leading to increased lipolysis, ketone production, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis. The presence of ketonemia in a young patient with rapid symptom onset supports this mechanism.
options.would_make_right: Change the age to a teenager and add history of autoimmune disease (eg, elevated anti-GAD antibodies) while keeping ketonemia and anion gap acidosis.

options.text: Insulin receptor resistance causing impaired glucose uptake
options.why: Insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes typically does not cause ketonemia with anion gap metabolic acidosis unless there is severe stress or profound insulin deficiency. The vignette emphasizes active ketone production.
options.would_make_right: Remove ketones and replace beta-hydroxybutyrate with normal values, while describing longer, less acute symptoms more consistent with type 2 diabetes.

options.text: Defective insulin secretion with preserved insulin action
options.why: Partial insulin secretory defects without severe insulin deficiency usually do not produce marked ketonemia and anion gap metabolic acidosis. The vignette already demonstrates significant absolute insulin lack physiology.
options.would_make_right: Lower glucose substantially (eg, ~180-250 mg/dL) and change beta-hydroxybutyrate to normal, while describing stable weight without acute acidosis.

options.text: Excess cortisol production leading to increased gluconeogenesis
options.why: Cortisol excess causes hyperglycemia via gluconeogenesis but does not primarily lead to ketonemia with anion gap metabolic acidosis in this presentation. The key abnormality is ketone-driven acidosis from insulin deficiency.
options.would_make_right: Add physical findings of Cushing syndrome (eg, proximal muscle weakness, moon facies) and replace ketonemia with elevated cortisol/low ACTH while normalizing anion gap.

options.text: Increased glucagon secretion causing hepatic glycogenolysis
options.why: Glucagon excess can raise blood glucose, but it is not the typical mechanism for ketonemia and anion gap metabolic acidosis caused by insulin deficiency. No findings suggest a glucagon-secreting tumor or similar process.
options.would_make_right: Include a pancreatic mass with markedly elevated glucagon levels and remove ketones/anion gap acidosis, leaving isolated hyperglycemia.

questions.rule: In acute symptomatic hyperglycemia, ketonemia with anion gap acidosis points to absolute insulin deficiency (type 1).
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine (Diabetes Mellitus) and Biochemistry/Pathology (Anion gap metabolic acidosis)
ADA Standards of Care (DKA diagnostic features)

questions.hook: “Why does this patient have a diastolic murmur that gets louder when the heart rate slows?”
questions.vignette: A 68-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea for 6 months. She reports palpitations but no chest pain. Vitals: BP 128/76 mmHg, HR 86/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 94% on room air. Cardiac exam shows an irregularly irregular rhythm. A low-pitched, mid-diastolic murmur is heard best at the cardiac apex with the patient in the left lateral position. An additional high-frequency sound follows S2. Transthoracic echocardiography shows thickened mitral valve leaflets with restricted opening. What maneuver will most increase the murmur’s intensity?
questions.short_vignette: 68F with dyspnea, AF, apex mid-diastolic rumble plus opening snap; echo shows restricted mitral leaflet opening. Which maneuver increases murmur intensity?
questions.stem: Which maneuver would most increase the intensity of her murmur?

options.why: Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance and increases venous return, raising left atrial pressure and transmit flow across a stenotic mitral valve, making the diastolic murmur louder.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to state the murmur is a mitral stenosis diastolic rumble with opening snap, then ask specifically for a maneuver that increases venous return/left atrial pressure (squatting).

options.why: Standing decreases venous return, lowering left atrial pressure and reducing flow across the stenotic mitral valve, so the murmur would lessen.
options.would_make_right: If squatting (A) were replaced by standing (B) in the question with the same vignette, B would become correct.

options.text: Instructing her to perform a Valsalva maneuver
options.why: Valsalva decreases venous return (especially with strain), reducing mitral flow and diminishing the intensity of the diastolic murmur.
options.would_make_right: If the vignette’s question instead asked for a maneuver that decreases venous return, then Valsalva would be the correct choice.

options.text: Administering a beta-agonist that increases heart rate
options.why: In mitral stenosis, tachycardia shortens diastole, reducing time for blood to flow across the stenotic valve, so the murmur becomes softer.
options.would_make_right: If the vignette asked which intervention decreases murmur intensity in mitral stenosis, then increasing heart rate would be correct.

options.why: Reducing preload lowers left atrial pressure and mitral transvalvular flow, which would weaken the murmur rather than increase it.
options.would_make_right: If the vignette asked which maneuver decreases murmur intensity, nitrate-induced preload reduction would make E correct.

questions.rule: In mitral stenosis, maneuvers that increase left atrial pressure or prolong diastole increase the murmur intensity.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiology: Valvular Heart Disease
ACC/AHA guideline discussion of physical exam maneuvers for valvular lesions

questions.topic: Acute Coronary Syndrome: NSTEMI vs Unstable Angina
questions.hook: You can’t assume chest pain with no ST elevation is unstable angina—troponin decides NSTEMI.
questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man with hypertension presents to the ED with 40 minutes of substernal chest pressure at rest. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Vitals: BP 146/88 mmHg, HR 104/min, RR 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, T 36.8°C. ECG shows 1 mm ST depression in leads V4-V6 without ST-segment elevation. Serum high-sensitivity troponin I returns at 0.9 ng/mL (reference <0.04 ng/mL). What diagnosis best fits this presentation?
questions.short_vignette: 58M with rest chest pressure, ST depression (no ST elevation), high-sensitivity troponin I elevated to 0.9 ng/mL.
questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains his presentation?

options.why: NSTEMI presents with evidence of myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin) along with ischemic symptoms. ST elevation is absent.
options.would_make_right: Change troponin to be clearly elevated (e.g., 0.9 ng/mL) while keeping ECG without ST elevation.

options.why: Unstable angina causes ischemic symptoms and ECG changes but does not elevate troponin because there is no measurable myocardial necrosis.
options.would_make_right: Set high-sensitivity troponin I to remain normal (e.g., 0.02 ng/mL) with the same ECG findings.

options.why: STEMI requires ST-segment elevation on ECG, which is explicitly not present here.
options.would_make_right: Modify the ECG description to include ST-segment elevation (e.g., ≥1 mm in contiguous leads) while keeping troponin elevated.

options.why: Acute pericarditis typically has diffuse, pleuritic pain and ECG changes such as diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not regional ST depression plus troponin-defined NSTEMI.
options.would_make_right: Replace symptoms with pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward and describe diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

options.why: Pulmonary embolism may cause chest pain and tachycardia, but the vignette lacks supportive features (eg, hypoxemia, risk factors) and shows troponin elevation with ischemic ECG changes consistent with ACS.
options.would_make_right: Add hypoxemia and tachycardia with high clinical suspicion for PE (e.g., SpO2 90% and ECG showing S1Q3T3) while removing ischemic ECG pattern.
